title: Triangulation
summary: Losing a move on purpose so that the opponent is left with the wrong turn.
part.zugzwang.title: Zugzwang
part.zugzwang.summary: A great position with the wrong side to move, and why chess has no pass.
part.triangle.title: The triangle
part.triangle.summary: Three neighbouring squares, three moves, and the same position comes back with Black to move.
part.kasparov.title: Triangulation with Black
part.kasparov.summary: Either side can triangulate, even with the king far from the enemy pawns.
part.defend.title: When the triangle is not enough
part.defend.summary: A defender with as many squares as the attacker answers each one and draws.
step.t_zugzwang: Imagine it is Black to move. Where can the black king go, and what does the white king do in each case?
step.t_zugzwang.hint1: Count the black king's squares. The c6-pawn covers two of them, and the white king covers others.
step.t_zugzwang.hint2: Only b8, c8 and d8 are left. From any of them, the white king gets in on b6 or d6.
step.zugzwang: With Black to move, it is over. The black king cannot go to b7 or d7, which the c6-pawn covers, nor to b6 or d6, next to my king. That leaves b8, c8 and d8, and from any of them he opens the door: my king goes to b6 or d6, wins the a6-pawn or walks the c6-pawn home. That is zugzwang: having to move is the misfortune.
step.pass: Now the same position with White to move. Kb6 and Kd6 do not exist, they are next to the black king; b5 is covered by the a6-pawn. If my king goes to b4, c4 or d4, the c6-pawn falls. I would love to say "pass", but chess does not allow it. So I will lose a move some other way. That is what this lesson is about.
step.d_zugzwang: First look at the prize: the position with Black to move. I play both sides.
step.d_zugzwang.m1: The black king picks c8. Any square comes to the same.
step.d_zugzwang.m2: My king steps into b6. From here it watches a6, c7 and b7.
step.d_zugzwang.m3: Black tries d8 to hold the pawn.
step.d_zugzwang.m4: Kb7: now c8 is mine too. The c6-pawn has a free road.
step.d_zugzwang.m5: The black king still tries to come closer.
step.d_zugzwang.m8: A queen. All because Black had the move.
step.zzMove: White to play and win. The black king is on c7 and yours on d5. Put Black in zugzwang, then go in.
step.zzMove.hint: Take the king to c5, facing the black king and protecting the c6-pawn. Then go in via b6.
step.zzMove.done: That's it. Kc5 left Black with the move, the white king got to b6 and the a6-pawn fell. Two pawns up, the rest is technique.
step.t_triangle: This is the key position of the lesson. White to move. You want the zugzwang position, but with Black to move. How?
step.t_triangle.hint1: Compare the two kings' squares. Where can the white king walk without letting go of the c6-pawn? And the black king, without letting go of c8?
step.t_triangle.hint2: The white king has d5, c4 and d4, three squares that touch each other. The black king has c8 and d8, and that is all.
step.t_triangle.hint3: A round trip over three squares takes three moves. Over two squares, it takes two. Who arrives late?
step.pairs: Think in pairs. White king on c5 and black king on c7, Black to move: zugzwang, you have seen it. The same holds for d6 against d8, and for d5 against c8. These squares correspond: when my king stands on one, the black king must stand on the other, with me to move. Here we have d5 against c8, and it is my move. The right pair with the wrong turn.
step.why: The way out is the triangle. My king goes from d5 to c4, from c4 to d4, and from d4 back to d5: three moves, and at the end d5 guards the pawn again. The black king would like to do the same, but he cannot: b7 and d7 are covered by the c6-pawn, and c7 is a poisoned square, because there he attacks the pawn, but my king returns to c5 or d5 and it is his move. That leaves c8, d8 and b8, where he can only swing back and forth in twos. Three moves against two: at the end of the trip, he is the one to move.
step.d_triangle: Watch the whole triangle and what comes after.
step.d_triangle.m1: Kc4, the first corner. The c6-pawn is safe: on c8, the black king cannot reach it.
step.d_triangle.m3: Kd4, the second corner. From d4 I watch c5, d5 and e5.
step.d_triangle.m4: The black king goes back to c8. He has no third square.
step.d_triangle.m5: Kd5, and the trip is complete: the starting position, now with Black to move.
step.d_triangle.m6: If ...Kd8, Kd6; if ...Kb8, Kd6 as well. Black tries c7.
step.d_triangle.m7: Kc5: the zugzwang from the first part.
step.d_triangle.m8: The black king has to leave c7.
step.d_triangle.m9: Kb6, and the a6-pawn falls. We win.
step.triangleMove: White to play and win. Make the triangle and come back to d5 with Black to move.
step.triangleMove.hint: Use c4 and d4, the two squares behind d5. When the black king goes to c7, answer on c5.
step.triangleMove.done: Perfect. Three moves to get back to d5, and the black king, with two squares, arrived late. Now he is in zugzwang.
step.t_kasparov: Alburt against Kasparov, 1978. Kasparov, with Black, was to move here. Black wants to reach g3 and take the h3-pawn. What stops him, and how does he solve it?
step.t_kasparov.hint1: Imagine White to move. The white king has little room: e2 and g2 are covered by the f3-pawn.
step.t_kasparov.hint2: With White to move, Kf2 is met by Kf4 and the white king has to give way. So Black wants this position with White to move.
step.kasparov: This is the same problem on the other side of the board. If White were to move, he would be lost: Kf2, Kf4, and the white king has to leave the road to g3 open. But it is Black's move. Kasparov made the triangle e4, f5, e5 and came back to e4 in three moves. The white king went to g1 and back to f1 in two, and the position repeated with White to move. The f3-pawn helps: it covers e2 and g2, and the white king has little room.
step.d_kasparov: First what Kasparov wanted: the same position with White to move.
step.d_kasparov.m2: Kf4: opposition. The white king has to step aside.
step.d_kasparov.m3: Kf1. Any other move opens the door as well.
step.d_kasparov.m4: Kg3, and the h3-pawn is lost.
step.d_kasparov.m5: The white king cannot get back in time.
step.d_kasparov.m6: The black pawns run, and the white king cannot catch them. That is why Alburt resigned.
step.kasparovMove: Black to play and win. Make Kasparov's triangle and come back to e4 with White to move.
step.kasparovMove.hint: Use f5 and e5. Once you are back on e4 and the white king goes to f2, stand face to face with it.
step.kasparovMove.done: Exactly, like Kasparov. In the game, after Kf5 and Ke5, Alburt resigned: he saw Kf4 coming.
step.t_defend: Now you defend. Another structure: pawns on e5 and e6. The white king prowls on the queenside looking for a way in. Black to move. Where does the black king belong?
step.t_defend.hint1: The white king can wait on b4 and c4. How many waiting squares do you have?
step.t_defend.hint2: You have two as well: b8 and c8. When the white king steps up to the fifth rank, face it.
step.defend: Here the triangle does not work, because the black king has enough squares. When the white king stands on c5 or b5, the black king faces it on c7 or b7. When White drops back to b4 or c4, Black goes back to the eighth rank and waits between b8 and c8. Two waiting squares against two: every white king move has an answer.
step.d_defend.m1: The white king drops back to b4, to lose a move.
step.d_defend.m2: Kb8: the black king drops back too.
step.d_defend.m3: Kc4, the second corner of the triangle.
step.d_defend.m4: Kc8: Black has a second corner too.
step.d_defend.m5: Kb5, back on the fifth rank.
step.d_defend.m8: Kc7, face to face again. Same position, same side to move: nothing has changed.
step.defendMove: Black to play and draw. Answer every white king move with your own square.
step.defendMove.hint: On the eighth rank, switch between b8 and c8. When the white king steps up to the fifth, step up to the seventh, facing it.
step.defendMove.done: Well done. Every square of the white king had its answer, and the triangle was useless. A draw.
step.recap: Three rules to take away. First: if the position is good but the turn is bad, lose a move. Second: the triangle does that, three neighbouring squares and three moves to come back; the other king needs three squares to copy it and hardly ever has them. Third: count the waiting squares on both sides. Whoever has more wins the fight for tempi; the defender only survives with the same number, answering square by square.
step.finish: Now play the key position to the end. Triangle, zugzwang, and only then go in.
ex.e05: White to play and win. The advance with check is tempting.
ex.e05.hint: After c6+? the black king goes to c8 and draws. Look for a triangle around d5.
ex.e05.solution: Ke5, Kd4 and Kd5: the triangle d5, e5, d4 gives back the position with Black to move. After ...Kc6, Kd4! is the only move. On the first move Kc4, Kd4 and Ke4 also win; only c6+? draws.
ex.e11: Black to play and win. In this position, in a game between Yudasin and Osnos, Black agreed to a draw. There is more here.
ex.e11.hint: The f-pawn is not yet where it needs to be. Take it to f3 with the king close by and you will recognise Kasparov's position.
ex.e11.solution: Ke4! and, after Ke2, f4 and f3: with the pawn on f3 and the king on e4 against the king on f1, this is the Alburt–Kasparov position with Black to move. Then the triangle: Kf5, Ke5 and Ke4, and the white king, unable to copy the walk, is left with the wrong turn and has to give up the h3-pawn. Ke5 and Kg5 also win on the first move.
ex.e04: White to play and win. Attacking the f7-pawn looks obvious. Watch out for the turn.
ex.e04.hint: The white king wants to be on g7 with Black to move. Get there another way.
ex.e04.solution: Kg8! (Kh8 also wins). If ...Ke6, Kg7! and now the zugzwang is Black's: the black king has to let go of f7. Kg7? straight away loses: after ...Ke6 it is the white king that must leave g7, and the f6-pawn falls.
ex.e12: White to play and win. Attacking the d4-pawn with the king is the natural move. Is it the right one?
ex.e12.hint: Kc4? lets the black king into e4, and the d-pawn runs. King on d3 against king on e5 is reciprocal zugzwang: return to d3 in three moves.
ex.e12.solution: Kd2! (Kc2 and Ke2 also win) and, after ...Kf6, Ke2 and Kd3: the same position with Black to move. The black king only has f6 and d6 to wait on, and any step away from e5 lets a white pawn advance: f6 or g5. Kc4? Ke4! only draws: f6 d3, Kc3 Ke3, and both pawns promote.
ex.e13: Black to play and draw. The kings are far from the pawns, and the white king has plenty of squares to walk round. Only one move holds.
ex.e13.hint: Here the triangle does not help the attacker: the black king has plenty of squares too. Take the distant opposition and answer square for square.
ex.e13.solution: Kg7! (the only move). After Kf3, Kf7! After Kf4, Kf6 (or Kf8); after Ke4, Ke7! After Kd4, Kd7 (or Kd8). The black king stays on the same file as the white one, with an odd number of squares between them, and reaches c7 or b6 in time when the white king tries the queenside. Kg5? Kf3! and the opposition is White's: Kf5 Ke3, Ke5 Kd3, and the white king gets in via c3 and b4.
ex.e10: White to play and win. Only one move keeps the win.
ex.e10.hint: If it were Black to move in this very position, the black king would have to leave e4. Come back to e2 in three moves.
ex.e10.solution: Ke1! and, after ...Kf5, Kd2 and Ke2: the triangle e2, e1, d2, and the same position with Black to move. The black king only has f5 and the advance d4, and both lose. Any other first move draws.
ex.e16: White to play and win. The g6- and h5-pawns tie the black king down, but the e4-pawn wants to run. Only one move wins.
ex.e16.hint: The key position is king on f4 against king on f6, with the black pawn on d5: Black to move loses, White to move only draws. Reach f4 with the right turn: spend one move more on the way.
ex.e16.solution: Kg4! Kf6 (everything loses) Kg3! The king went from h3 to g3 in two moves instead of one, and now it is Black who has to move. If ...d5, Kf4! and the black king must give up f6 or the e4-pawn: ...Kg7 Kxe4, or ...Ke7 and the white king gets in via g5. If ...e3, Kf3 and the pawn falls with the black king still tied to g7 and f6. Kg3? at once: d5! Kf4 Kf6, the same position with White to move, and it is a draw.
ex.e09: Grigoriev's study. White to play and win. The white king wants to reach e2, e3 or d4.
ex.e09.hint: The advance d4? draws. The black king only has f3 and f4 to wait on; the white king has several squares behind. Take a walk.
ex.e09.solution: Kc2, Kb3, Kb2 and Kc2 again: the white king goes round and the black king, with only f3 and f4, arrives late. After Kd2 and ...Kf4, Ke2! takes a key square. On the first move d4? and Ke1? draw; in the middle of the walk other king moves work too.
key.zugzwang: The position White wants: the kings face each other and Black is to move. The black king has to give way, and the white one walks in.
key.triangle: White has the right position but the wrong side to move. The white king walks round a triangle of three neighbouring squares; the black one, with only two squares to shuffle between, hands the move back.
key.alburtKasparov: Alburt against Kasparov, 1978: the young Kasparov made the triangle with his king far from his own pawns, returned to the same position with the right side to move, and Alburt resigned.
key.defend: When the triangle is not enough: the black king has enough waiting squares and answers every white step. Without zugzwang, it is a draw.
history: To triangulate is to lose a move on purpose. The king walks round three neighbouring squares, in a triangle, and comes back to where it was; the enemy king, with less room, cannot copy it, and ends up with the wrong side to move. Walking in a circle to get back to the same spot feels strange, which is why so many players miss the manoeuvre even with the win in hand. In 1978 the young Kasparov beat Lev Alburt with a king triangle made far from his own pawns. The idea is not limited to pawn endings: at the 1965 Candidates, Spassky triangulated with his king in a rook ending against Tal and went on to play for the world title. Dvoretsky gave it its own section in his endgame manual.
practice: Now the real ending, from the start: king on c5 against king on c7, and it is your move. Only one move keeps the pawn. Find it, make the triangle and win. Choose the pace and go.
